# nyc

[![ci](https://github.com/istanbuljs/nyc/actions/workflows/ci.yaml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/bcoe/c8/actions/workflows/ci.yaml)
[![NPM version](https://img.shields.io/npm/v/nyc.svg)](https://www.npmjs.com/package/nyc)
[![Conventional Commits](https://img.shields.io/badge/Conventional%20Commits-1.0.0-yellow.svg)](https://conventionalcommits.org)

_Having problems? want to contribute? join our [community slack](https://devtoolscommunity.herokuapp.com)_.

Istanbul's state of the art command line interface, with support for:

* applications that spawn subprocesses.
* source mapped coverage of Babel and TypeScript projects

## How Istanbul works

Istanbul instruments your ES5 and ES2015+ JavaScript code with line counters, so that you can track how well your unit-tests exercise your codebase.

The `nyc` command-line-client for Istanbul works well with most JavaScript testing frameworks: tap, mocha, AVA, etc.

## Installation & Usage

Use your package manager to add it as a dev dependency: `npm i -D nyc` or `yarn add -D nyc`.
You can use nyc to call npm scripts (assuming they don't already have nyc executed in them), like so (replace `mocha` with your test runner everywhere you see it):

```json
{
  "scripts": {
    "test": "mocha",
    "coverage": "nyc npm run test"
  }
}
```

You can use also `npx` instead of installing nyc as a dependency, but you might get updates you are not ready for; to get around this, pin to a specific major version by specifying, e.g. `nyc@14`.

```json
{
  "scripts": {
    "test": "npx nyc@latest mocha"
  }
}
```

This is a good way of testing upcoming releases of nyc, usually on the `next` tag.

**Note**: If you use [`jest`](https://npm.im/jest) or [`tap`](https://www.node-tap.org/), you do not need to install `nyc`.
Those runners already have the IstanbulJS libraries to provide coverage for you.
Follow their documentation to enable and configure coverage reporting.

## Configuring `nyc`

nyc accepts a wide variety of configuration arguments, run `npx nyc --help` for thorough documentation.

Configuration arguments on the command-line should be provided prior to the program that nyc is executing.
As an example, the following command executes `ava`, and indicates to nyc that it should output both an `lcov` (`lcov.info` + html report) and a `text-summary` coverage report.

```shell
nyc --reporter=lcov --reporter=text-summary ava
```

### Babel projects

Please start with the pre-configured [`@istanbuljs/nyc-config-babel`] preset.
You can add your custom configuration options as shown below.

### TypeScript projects

Please start with the pre-configured [`@istanbuljs/nyc-config-typescript`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@istanbuljs/nyc-config-typescript) preset.

#### Adding your overrides

nyc allows you to inherit other configurations using the key `extends` in the `package.json` stanza, `.nycrc`, or YAML files.
You can then add the specific configuration options you want that aren't in that particular shared config, e.g.

```json
{
  "extends": "@istanbuljs/nyc-config-typescript",
  "all": true,
  "check-coverage": true
}
```

### Configuration files

Any configuration options that can be set via the command line can also be specified in the `nyc` stanza of your package.json, or within a separate configuration file - a variety of flavors are available:

| File name        | File Association                            |
|------------------|---------------------------------------------|
| `.nycrc`         | JSON                                        |
| `.nycrc.json`    | JSON                                        |
| `.nycrc.yaml`    | YAML                                        |
| `.nycrc.yml`     | YAML                                        |
| `nyc.config.js`  | ESM / CommonJS export based on package type |
| `nyc.config.cjs` | CommonJS export                             |
| `nyc.config.mjs` | ESM export                                  |

### Common Configuration Options

See `nyc --help` for all options available.
You can set these in any of the files listed above, or from the command line.
This table is a quick TLDR for the rest of this readme and there are more advanced docs available.

| Option name | Description | Type | Default |
| ----------- | ----------- | ---- | ------- |
| `all` | Whether or not to instrument all files (not just the ones touched by your test suite) | `Boolean` | `false` |
| `check-coverage` | Check whether coverage is within thresholds, fail if not | `Boolean` | `false` |
| `extension` | List of extensions that nyc should attempt to handle in addition to `.js` | `Array<String>` | `['.js', '.cjs', '.mjs', '.ts', '.tsx', '.jsx']` |
| `include` | See [selecting files for coverage] for more info | `Array<String>` | `['**']`|
| `exclude` | See [selecting files for coverage] for more info | `Array<String>` | [list](https://github.com/istanbuljs/schema/blob/master/default-exclude.js) |
| `reporter` | May be set to a [built-in coverage reporter](https://istanbul.js.org/docs/advanced/alternative-reporters/) or an npm package (dev)dependency | `Array<String>` | `['text']` |
| `report-dir` | Where to put the coverage report files | `String` | `./coverage` |
| `skip-full` | Don't show files with 100% statement, branch, and function coverage | `Boolean` | `false` |
| `temp-dir` | Directory to output raw coverage information to | `String` | `./.nyc_output` |

Configuration can also be provided by `nyc.config.js` if programmed logic is required:

```js
'use strict';

const defaultExclude = require('@istanbuljs/schema/default-exclude');
const isWindows = require('is-windows');

let platformExclude = [
  isWindows() ? 'lib/posix.js' : 'lib/win32.js'
];

module.exports = {
  exclude: platformExclude.concat(defaultExclude)
};
```

### Publish and reuse your nyc configuration(s)

To publish and reuse your own `nyc` configuration, simply create an npm module that exports your JSON config (via [`index.json`](https://github.com/istanbuljs/istanbuljs/blob/master/packages/nyc-config-typescript/) or a CJS [`index.js`](https://github.com/istanbuljs/istanbuljs/blob/master/packages/nyc-config-hook-run-in-this-context/)).

A more advanced use case would be to combine multiple shared configs in a `nyc.config.js` file:

```js
'use strict';

const babelConfig = require('@istanbuljs/nyc-config-babel');
const hookRunInThisContextConfig = require('@istanbuljs/nyc-config-hook-run-in-this-context');

module.exports = {
  ...babelConfig,
  ...hookRunInThisContextConfig,
  all: true,
  'check-coverage': true
};
```

## Selecting files for coverage

By default, nyc only collects coverage for source files that are visited during a test.
It does this by watching for files that are `require()`'d during the test.
When a file is `require()`'d, nyc creates and returns an instrumented version of the source, rather than the original.
Only source files that are visited during a test will appear in the coverage report and contribute to coverage statistics.

nyc will instrument all files if the `--all` flag is set or if running `nyc instrument`.
In this case all files will appear in the coverage report and contribute to coverage statistics.

nyc will only collect coverage for files that are located under `cwd`, and then only files with extensions listed in the `extension` array.

You can reduce the set of instrumented files by adding `include` and `exclude` filter arrays to your config.
These allow you to shape the set of instrumented files by specifying glob patterns that can filter files from the default instrumented set.
The `exclude` array may also use exclude negated glob patterns, these are specified with a `!` prefix, and can restore sub-paths of excluded paths.

Globs are matched using [minimatch](https://www.npmjs.com/package/minimatch).

We use the following process to remove files from consideration:

1. Limit the set of instrumented files to those files in paths listed in the `include` array.
2. Remove any files that are found in the `exclude` array.
3. Restore any exclude negated files that have been excluded in step 2.

# Producing instrumented source

The `nyc instrument` command can produce instrumented source files.
These files are suitable for client side deployment during end to end testing.
You can either pre-instrument your source, or write instrumented source to a stream.

Run `nyc instrument --help` to display a full list of available command options.

## Pre-instrumented source

You can create pre-instrumented source code by running:

```bash
nyc instrument <input> [output]
```

`<input>` can be any file or directory within the project root directory.
The `[output]` directory is optional and can be located anywhere, if not set the instrumented code will be sent to `stdout`.
For example, `nyc instrument . ./output` will produce instrumented versions of any source files it finds in `.` and store them in `./output`.

The `--delete` option will remove the existing output directory before instrumenting.

The `--in-place` option will allow you to run the instrument command.

The `--complete-copy` option will copy all remaining files from the `input` directory to the `output` directory.
When using `--complete-copy` nyc will not copy the contents of a `.git` folder to the output directory.

**Note:** `--complete-copy` will dereference any symlinks during the copy process, this may stop scripts running properly from the output directory.

## Streaming instrumentation

`nyc instrument <input>` will stream instrumented source directly to `stdout` and that output can then be piped to another process.
You can use this behaviour to create a server that dynamically instruments files on request.
The following example shows streaming instrumentation middleware capable of instrumenting files on request.

```javascript
app.use((req, res, next) => {
  const myOptions = ""
  const filename = myHelper.getFilename(req)
  const nyc = cp.spawn(`nyc instrument ${myOptions} ${filename}`)
  nyc.stdout.pipe(res)
})
```

# Profiling:

The self-coverage tool can provide a [fairly interesting information on how nyc performs](https://github.com/bcoe/nyc/pull/101#issuecomment-165337057) in real world test suites. Doing this is a bit involved, detailed steps follow.

*Note:* This assumes your locally cloned development version of `nyc` is in `/user/dev/nyc`, and that you are profiling against the AVA test suite in `/user/dev/ava`. Adapt as required.

## Initial Setup (NYC)

We must use `npm link`, and ensure we have fresh "self-coverage" scripts generated.

```sh
# Go to the local clone of nyc
cd /user/dev/nyc

# Link the local clone globally
npm link

# Create the self-coverage instrumented files
node ./build-self-coverage
```

## Initial Setup (Test Project)

```sh
# CD to the real world test suite you want to profile against
cd /user/dev/ava

# Link the globally linked nyc into your local node_modules
npm link nyc
```

This will likely not work with `tap --coverage`, since tap will try to use its own older copy of nyc instead of your globally linked one. Modify the test script in your test project so it uses the `nyc` binary directly, and disable `tap`s version with the `--no-cov` flag:

`package.json`:

```json
{
  "scripts" : {
    "test": "nyc tap --no-cov test/*.js"
  }
}
```

## Each Run

```sh
# Clear existing self coverage (`trash` ~== `rm -rf`)
cd /user/dev/nyc
trash ./.self_coverage

# Clear the `.nyc_cache` folder in your test project
cd /user/dev/ava
trash ./.nyc_cache

# Run your test suite
npm test

# Go back to the `nyc` folder and create a self-coverage report
cd /user/dev/nyc
npm run report
```

A detailed profile of your test run now exists in `/user/dev/nyc/coverage/lcov-report`

*Note:* `trash` is a safer version of `rm -rf`. Install via `npm i -g trash-cli`. [More info](https://github.com/sindresorhus/guides/blob/master/how-not-to-rm-yourself.md).

## WARNING: Self coverage can cause some confusing problems.

If `index.covered.js` exists, it will be used instead of the normal file. This means your changes to `index.js` will not have an effect until you recreate or delete the self coverage files. Unless you are trying to do some profiling, you should probably delete them so the regular files are used.

You can delete the self coverage scripts and use the regular ones as follows:

```sh
# Go to nyc directory and remove the self coverage scripts
cd /user/dev/nyc
npm run clean
```

You can rerun `node ./build-self-coverage` scripts as desired to re-enable self-coverage.

# Integrating with codecov.io

[codecov](https://codecov.io/) is a great tool for adding coverage reports to your GitHub project, even viewing them inline on GitHub with a [browser extension](https://docs.codecov.io/docs/browser-extension).

## Quick start

Assuming your `npm test` does not run `nyc` and you have the `npx` executable (npm v5.2+), have your CI runner execute the following:

```shell
npx nyc --reporter=lcov npm test && npx codecov
```

## Without `npx` - Travis CI example using npm scripts

1. add the codecov and nyc dependencies:

  ```shell
  npm install codecov nyc --save-dev
  ```

2. update the scripts in your package.json to include these lines (replace `mocha` with your test runner):

  ```json
  {
     "scripts": {
       "test": "nyc --reporter=lcov mocha",
       "coverage": "codecov"
     }
  }
  ```

3. For private repos, add the environment variable `CODECOV_TOKEN` to Travis CI.

4. add the following to your `.travis.yml`:

  ```yaml
  after_success: npm run coverage
  ```

# Integrating with coveralls.io

[coveralls.io](https://coveralls.io) is a great tool for adding
coverage reports to your GitHub project. Here's how to get nyc
integrated with coveralls and travis-ci.org:

1. add the coveralls and nyc dependencies to your module:

  ```shell
  npm install coveralls nyc --save-dev
  ```

2. update the scripts in your package.json to include these bins:

  ```json
  {
     "scripts": {
       "test": "nyc mocha",
       "coverage": "nyc report --reporter=text-lcov | coveralls"
     }
  }
  ```

3. For private repos, add the environment variable `COVERALLS_REPO_TOKEN` to Travis CI.

4. add the following to your `.travis.yml`:

  ```yaml
  after_success: npm run coverage
  ```

That's all there is to it!

> Note: by default coveralls.io adds comments to pull-requests on GitHub, this can feel intrusive. To disable this, click on your repo on coveralls.io and uncheck `LEAVE COMMENTS?`.

report.overview: nyc is Istanbul’s JavaScript coverage CLI for developers who want to run existing test commands, collect coverage across subprocesses, and enforce coverage thresholds. It instruments source through Node loading hooks or an offline instrument command, persists per-process coverage, then merges and remaps results into configurable reports. At commit 908620475199fa7b9ea0ea8b21d6d8ad6921e3ae, the package is version 18.0.0 and supports Node 20 or Node 22 and newer.
report.agent_prompt:
You are onboarding to nyc at commit 908620475199fa7b9ea0ea8b21d6d8ad6921e3ae. This is a CommonJS npm package exposing the NYC class through index.js and the nyc executable through bin/nyc.js. It instruments JavaScript for Istanbul coverage, handles subprocess collection, persists coverage JSON, remaps source locations, creates reports, and checks thresholds. It also supports offline instrumentation and merging raw coverage files.

Start with package.json, bin/nyc.js, index.js, lib/config-util.js, lib/process-args.js, and lib/commands/helpers.js. Configuration loading is delegated to @istanbuljs/load-nyc-config; CLI options come from @istanbuljs/schema. Preserve argument separation between nyc and the command being measured. The four explicit commands are report, check-coverage, instrument, and merge; their names appear in multiple dispatch locations.

Trace the runtime before changing it. main() parses configuration, selects an instrumenter, prepares temporary storage, establishes environment and preload propagation, optionally calls addAllFiles(), and invokes foregroundChild(). lib/wrap.js reconstructs child configuration and process ancestry, applies NYC_CONFIG_OVERRIDE, and calls NYC.wrap(). wrap() installs hooks and an exit callback. Loaded source passes through _handleJs(), exclusion filtering, extension transforms, and the instrumenter. Exit handling writes UUID-named coverage JSON and matching process metadata. The parent subsequently indexes processes, checks thresholds when requested, and reports unless silent.

For persistence or reporting work, inspect lib/source-maps.js and lib/hash.js. Coverage is held in __coverage__; cached runs attach contentHash for source-map recovery. Reporting loads and merges files, remaps coverage, optionally excludes after remapping, and invokes istanbul-reports factories. coverageFileLoad() catches failures and returns an empty object, so missing data may be quiet. Distinguish runtime working directory, configured project root, temporary storage, cache storage, and report destinations.

Tests use TAP 18, snapshots, subprocess fixtures, and generated self-coverage copies. Read .taprc, build-self-coverage.js, self-coverage-helper.js, and test/helpers/paths.js before selecting checks: tests generally target self-coverage rather than root source directly. The npm pretest lifecycle runs lint, cleanup, and instrumentation; posttest creates the coverage report. For authorized implementation work, use the smallest relevant TAP file after refreshing generated copies, then the existing npm test lifecycle as appropriate. Cleanup mutates files and must not run during a read-only audit.

This brief inspected tests and CI but executed neither. Test definitions do not establish passing results, and inspection is bounded. Ubuntu CI specifies Node 20 and 24; Windows uses lts/*, skips signal checks, and disables coverage enforcement through nyc.config.js. Preserve small diffs and existing style. Treat custom require modules, instrumenter modules, environment overrides, deletion flags, in-place instrumentation, and complete-copy as sensitive boundaries. Report risks as observations or hypotheses until verified; do not infer vulnerabilities, performance gains, or exhaustive coverage from source alone.

system_map.summary: The npm package contains a reusable NYC class, a CLI coordinator, child bootstrap modules, and four command handlers. Instrumentation, coverage merging, source-map transformation, reporting, and process indexing use separate Istanbul libraries. Runtime boundaries follow parent and child processes, with configuration propagated through environment variables and coverage exchanged through files. Packaging and CI describe an npm CLI distribution with generated self-coverage used during development.

claims.claim: package.json publishes NYC through index.js and the nyc executable through bin/nyc.js; its files allowlist contains index.js, bin JavaScript, and lib JavaScript.
bin/nyc.js main() coordinates normal command execution, while report, check-coverage, instrument, and merge are registered as yargs command modules.
NYC owns configuration, exclusions, extension transforms, cache state, SourceMaps, and ProcessInfo; it dynamically loads the selected instrumenter module.
Child collection supports node-preload plus process-on-spawn environment propagation, or spawn-wrap with bin/wrap.js calling runMain().
Coverage persistence uses UUID-named JSON files beneath the configured temporary directory and a processinfo subdirectory; ProcessDB writes an index and renders process trees.
Instrumentation delegates to istanbul-lib-instrument, while coverage maps, source-map stores, report contexts, and report factories come from distinct Istanbul packages.
The npm lifecycle runs Standard lint, cleanup, and self-instrumentation before TAP tests, then generates text and lcov self-coverage reports afterward.
The engine range is Node 20 or >=22; CI specifies Ubuntu Node 20 and 24 plus Windows lts/*, and release-please runs on main only for istanbuljs/nyc.

feature_catalog.summary: The primary interface wraps an existing executable or test runner to collect coverage. Users can control file selection, account for unloaded files, preload transpilers, and choose reports or threshold enforcement. Separate commands instrument source trees, regenerate reports, check stored coverage, and merge raw results. Source maps and documented external uploader workflows connect coverage to transpiled projects and hosted reporting services.

claims.claim: Normal CLI execution accepts a child command and preserves its arguments; --silent suppresses reporting, and --no-clean retains stored results across runs.

File selection supports include/exclude patterns, additional extensions, and optional node_modules inclusion; --all adds initial coverage for eligible unloaded files, including an explicit ESM reading branch.
--require loads additional modules for transpilation or other setup; configurable require and VM hooks support ordinary modules, RequireJS/AMD, and vm.runInContext workloads.
nyc instrument accepts a file or directory and writes transformed source to an output tree or stdout; options include complete-copy, explicit in-place operation, deletion, and exit-on-error.
nyc report invokes each configured reporter with watermarks, skipEmpty, skipFull, projectRoot, and terminal width; show-process-tree additionally renders stored process ancestry.
Coverage checks support lines, functions, branches, and statements globally or per file; a percentage below its threshold sets process.exitCode to 1 and prints a diagnostic.
nyc merge validates an input directory and writes combined Istanbul coverage to an output file defaulting to coverage.json; its builder defaults exclude-after-remap to false.
Source-map handling accepts inline maps or referenced .map files and optionally emits instrumented-code maps; Codecov and Coveralls integration docs invoke external uploaders on nyc report output.

data_flow.summary: Arguments and project configuration become an NYC configuration object before child execution. Environment variables carry that configuration and ancestry into child processes, while loading hooks transform eligible source into counter-bearing code. Counters become coverage JSON and process metadata at exit. Report and merge operations read these artifacts, recover source maps, combine counters, and produce reports, merged JSON, or failure status.

claims.claim: guessCWD() starts from its argument, NYC_CWD, or process.cwd(), searches upward for package.json, then processConfig() separates child arguments and passes nyc arguments to loadNycConfig().
setupOptions() converts schema property names to dashed CLI names, carries defaults and aliases, treats arrays as string options, and hides options outside their declared command scope.
The parent serializes argv into NYC_CONFIG and records process.cwd() in NYC_CWD; register-env snapshots selected variables and copies them into spawned environments.
lib/wrap.js parses NYC_CONFIG, marks child execution, records pid/ppid/parent UUID, consumes an external process ID, and merges NYC_CONFIG_OVERRIDE before constructing NYC.
Hooked code flows through _handleJs(), shouldInstrument(), extension lookup, caching-transform, and instrumentSync(); transform hashing includes filename metadata and a configuration/version salt.
coverageFinder() obtains __coverage__; writeCoverageFile() removes excluded entries, attaches available content hashes when caching, serializes coverage, then saves matching process metadata.
SourceMaps registers maps in memory or writes basename/hash .map cache files; coverage loading uses contentHash to reload maps and records failed map loads as false to avoid repeated reads.

getCoverageMapFromAllCoverageFiles() reads directory entries with CPU-count concurrency, merges loaded reports, remaps coverage, and optionally filters afterward; report() renders that map and merge writes it as JSON.

behavior_traces.summary: The source supports ordered walkthroughs of command startup, child instrumentation, persistence and reporting, and offline instrumentation. These traces describe execution order and conditional branches rather than observed runs. Threshold checks and reporting differ in order between normal execution and the standalone report command. The --all and merge branches reuse core collection machinery while changing their input and output boundaries.

claims.claim: Startup: cliWrapper(main) → configUtil()/processConfig() → guessCWD() → setupOptions() → argument separation → loadNycConfig() → final yargs parse; recognized subcommands return from main, while missing commands set exitCode 1 and show help.

Wrapped execution: main() selects Istanbul or noop → new NYC(argv) → reset() or createTempDirectory() → establishes preload modules or spawn-wrap → optionally addAllFiles() → foregroundChild(childArgs).

Child instrumentation: lib/wrap.js constructs NYC → wrap() publishes NYC_PROCESS_ID → installs require/VM hooks → registers the exit handler → loads additional spawn-wrap modules; hooked source then passes _handleJs() → _maybeInstrumentSource() → _transform() → instrumentSync().

Persistence: the alwaysLast signal-exit callback calls writeCoverageFile() → coverageFinder() → exclusion cleanup → optional contentHash attachment → synchronous UUID JSON write → ProcessInfo.saveSync().

Parent completion: foregroundChild callback combines exit status → removes watchdog artifacts → writeProcessIndex() → maybePurgeSourceMapCache() → optional checkCoverage() → report() unless silent; caught completion errors force a nonzero result.

Offline instrumentation: command handler validates input/output and deletion conditions → selects instrumenter → adjusts in-place settings → preloads modules → instrumentAllFiles(); directory mode globs eligible files, optionally copies the remaining tree, then transforms and writes files with original modes.

--all: addAllFiles() loads additional modules → enables fakeRequire → globs eligible sources → directly instruments ESM or reads other files through Module._extensions → stores lastFileCoverage with all:true → disables fakeRequire → writes coverage.

Stored-result commands: report handler calls report() before optional checkCoverage(); merge handler validates the input directory, creates the output parent, loads/merges/remaps coverage through getCoverageMapFromAllCoverageFiles(), then writes JSON.

testing_signals.summary: Tests and CI were inspected, not executed; test existence establishes intended checks, not passing results. TAP tests combine direct NYC calls, spawned CLI fixtures, and output snapshots. Development tests generally target generated self-coverage copies, with a separate coverage variable and exit writer. Coverage inspection is bounded, and explicit Windows branches and ignored error paths limit what the configured checks establish.

claims.claim: package.json specifies TAP ^18.7.2 and Standard lint; .taprc disables TAP coverage, excludes helper/fixture paths, sets one job and a 360-second timeout, and preloads self-coverage-helper.js. These settings and CI were inspected only.

build-self-coverage.js instruments runtime files into self-coverage using ___NYC_SELF_COVERAGE___; test helper paths resolve the generated CLI, and self-coverage-helper writes that separate global coverage at exit.

CLI integration tests define checks for threshold success/failure, failing child status, configuration precedence, argument forwarding, process trees, and both spawn-wrap settings; testSuccess asserts zero status, empty stderr, and a stdout snapshot.
test/instrument.js checks mode preservation, complete-copy, include/exclude behavior, explicit in-place operation, outside-root rejection, and deletion guards.
Collection tests assert zero counters for unloaded --all sources and nonzero counters after require(); cache tests run collision and identical-file fixtures and assert child status 0.

Source-map tests cover external/inline maps, cache-file creation, exclude-after-remap behavior, and --all in a module package; TypeScript tests run committed mapping.js with mapping enabled and disabled, rather than directly testing a TypeScript loader.

Process tests inspect matching UUID coverage/process files and external-ID indexing; SIGTERM/SIGINT tests return without assertions on Windows, and nyc.config.js disables threshold enforcement there despite configured 100% thresholds.

CI declares npm test on Ubuntu Node 20/24 and Windows lts/*, but suppressEPIPE and several parent-completion error branches are explicitly excluded from instrumentation; no execution results were collected.

risk_map.summary: The sensitive boundaries inspected are local module execution, environment propagation, process hooks, and filesystem operations. Findings below are source observations, not confirmed vulnerabilities. Coverage can become incomplete through permissive instrumentation failures or suppressed artifact-loading errors. Cleanup, tree copying, and global hook state deserve focused review because their effects extend beyond a single transformed file.

claims.claim: Configuration can select a dynamically required instrumenter, and --require modules execute in the parent or child setup paths; these are executable trust boundaries rather than data-only configuration.

reset() recursively removes the resolved temporary directory when NYC_CWD is absent; configured temporary/report paths are resolved without a containment check, while instrument --delete has a separate working-directory guard.

complete-copy globs dotfiles and copies files beyond the instrumentation selection, excluding .git and the output tree; docs explicitly state symlinks are dereferenced, so copy scope is broader than coverage scope.

_transformFactory() returns original source after instrumentation errors unless exitOnError is set; parser-plugin tests explicitly expect a successful uninstrumented result when the required plugin is unset.
coverageFiles() lists every directory entry, and coverageFileLoad() converts any read, parse, or cached-map reload error into {}; cached source-map read failures are also suppressed and remembered.

NYC_CONFIG and NYC_CONFIG_OVERRIDE are parsed without local validation in the child bootstrap, and overrides are serialized back into NYC_CONFIG; environment configuration controls the constructed NYC instance.

wrap() documents a spawn-wrap limitation in forcing NYC_PROCESS_ID propagation; hook installation, global coverage, and require-extension state are process-wide, and tests explicitly reset require caches/loaders between cases.

Legacy guidance remains alongside current implementation: coverageData() still carries a 'Remove from nyc v16' TODO, profiling docs discuss index.covered.js, and .travis.yml lists Node 8/10 despite the current Node 20/>=22 engine range.

extension_points.summary: Extensions enter through command modules, schema-derived options, configuration presets, preloaded modules, instrumenter factories, and reporter factories. NYC already centralizes the selection and transform pipeline, so additions should reuse those boundaries. Some extension contracts depend on external packages rather than a repository-local registry. Command dispatch and cache invalidation require coordinated changes across multiple files.

claims.claim: A command module exports command, describe, builder, and handler; adding a command requires coordinating yargs registration, process-args' recognized command list, and bin/nyc.js' early-return list.
CLI options are derived from schema.nyc.properties through setupOptions(); coverageVariable and global-scope options are explicitly blocked because they are not connected to the instrumenter.
Reusable configurations use extends and can be exported as JSON or JavaScript npm modules; processConfig() delegates configuration loading to @istanbuljs/load-nyc-config.
The instrumenter factory receives ignoreClassMethods, source-map production, compactness, comments, ESM parsing, and parser plugins; built-in adapters expose instrumentSync() and lastFileCoverage().

Additional extensions receive entries in the transforms table and hook registration; addAllFiles() can obtain transpiled source through Module._extensions, falling back to the .js loader when an extension is unknown.
--require is the module-setup extension point, with resolution attempted relative to NYC.cwd before fallback; non-spawn-wrap startup places these modules before lib/wrap.js in the preload list.

Reporter names are stored as an array and passed to istanbul-reports.create(); README documents built-in reporters and npm package reporters, with per-reporter presentation options passed at execution.

Instrumentation cache behavior has explicit extension-sensitive hooks: _createTransform() chooses eager or lazy factories, records hashes by filename, and Hash.salt() includes package versions and selected configuration values.

agent_handoff.summary: Begin with the CLI/core boundary and the generated self-coverage test setup before making changes. Keep configuration, argument routing, source selection, subprocess ancestry, and report remapping consistent. Tests and CI were inspected, not executed, and this brief is a bounded source investigation rather than exhaustive verification. Future checks should use existing npm/TAP machinery only when execution is authorized, with particular care around cleanup and source-mutating fixtures.

claims.claim: Read package.json, bin/nyc.js, index.js, and lib/config-util.js first: they define publication, orchestration, state ownership, and configuration dispatch. This handoff is based on inspected source and CI, with no tests executed.
Follow Standard JavaScript style and two-space, LF, UTF-8 EditorConfig settings; the lint script excludes snapshots, fixtures, and generated test build paths.

Before running a targeted TAP file after authorized edits, refresh self-coverage through the existing instrument script: tests resolve generated runtime copies, and build-self-coverage copies package.json for generated hash-version lookup.

Select tests by boundary: argument routing uses test/process-args.js, offline filesystem behavior uses test/instrument.js, and subprocess CLI behavior uses test/nyc-integration.js; npm test invokes the broader configured lifecycle.

Treat cleanup and tests as mutating operations: npm-run-clean.js recursively removes artifact/cache paths, instrument tests temporarily chmod fixtures, and add-all-files tests create and remove source fixtures.
Keep command names synchronized across parsing and dispatch, and preserve the distinction between nyc arguments and child arguments, including Node execArgv passed after --.

For cache/source-map edits, inspect Hash.salt(), filename hash tracking, contentHash persistence, and cached map reloading together; report filtering occurs after remapping only when excludeAfterRemap is enabled.

Account for platform limits when reporting verification: inspected CI covers Ubuntu Node 20/24 and Windows lts/*, signal tests bypass Windows, and configured 100% coverage checks are disabled there; none of these definitions proves a passing run.

public_export.note: Public corpus projection; embedded scan omits the local clone path. Hash identifies the original corpus record, not raw CLI stdout.
